intro:
These exercises move from picking the right long-lived transport to owning a single connection cleanly and then surviving the conditions that actually break WebSocket services in production: slow consumers, reconnect storms, protocol drift, and deploy-time shutdown. The through-line is the chapter's mental model, a connection as a small machine with one reader job, one writer job, and one application job in the middle, plus a set of explicit policies for what happens when something falls behind.

The payoff is a connection model you can reason about from the types alone. By the end you should be able to say, before a single client connects, who owns the read half, who owns the write half, what happens when a queue fills, how the protocol evolves under mixed clients, and what the server does during a drain. Every exercise here pins down one of those answers so it is a design decision rather than an emergency.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose WebSockets, SSE, polling, gRPC streaming, or a broker-backed edge fan-out
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from direction, pace, and durability rather than from the transport you reach for by habit. The four products map cleanly once you ask what each one actually needs.

The browser dashboard that only receives updates wants Server-Sent Events. It is one-directional push from server to client, SSE rides plain HTTP, browsers reconnect automatically with a built-in Last-Event-ID cursor, and you avoid the entire upgrade-split-heartbeat-close lifecycle a WebSocket forces on you. The tradeoff is real but acceptable here: SSE is text-framed and one-way, so the moment the client needs to send commands you would be tunneling them over a separate channel.

The collaborative editor wants a WebSocket. Both sides send commands continuously, latency matters, and you want full bidirectional state over a single connection with ordered frames. This is the one case where the cost of the WebSocket lifecycle is justified by the requirement, not by familiarity.

The internal polyglot stream between services wants gRPC streaming. The clients are services, not browsers, so browser support is irrelevant, and what matters is a versioned protobuf contract with generated stubs across languages and HTTP/2 flow control underneath. You trade away browser reachability for schema tooling and typed contracts, which is the right trade when no browser is involved.

The durable event feed where clients reconnect after long offline gaps wants a broker-backed replay surface (Kafka, NATS JetStream, or a durable log) as the real durability boundary, with whatever edge transport delivering live tail. A raw socket fan-out has no memory: once a frame is sent it is gone, so a client offline for an hour cannot catch up. Making the broker the source of truth gives you replay by offset; the WebSocket or SSE becomes just the live edge. The tradeoff is operational weight, you now run and reason about a broker, but durability across long disconnects is exactly what a direct socket cannot provide.
criteria: At least three of the four picks are deliberately not WebSockets: SSE for the dashboard, gRPC streaming for the service stream, and a broker for the durable feed.
Each choice is justified by pacing or durability (one-way push, long offline replay, typed cross-service contract), not by framework familiarity.
Tradeoffs named explicitly: SSE is one-way only, gRPC sacrifices browser support for schema tooling, and the broker adds operational weight in exchange for replay.

exerciseSolutions.title: Review explicit read/write ownership in one connection loop
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the two designs against the chapter's ownership boundary, the split into a read half and a write half after the upgrade, rather than against mutex overhead. The split design (one reader task, one application loop, one writer task) is the calm default, and the reasons line up with the chapter's three concerns: ordering, shutdown, and observability.

Frame ordering and close behavior are easier to reason about in the split design because exactly one task owns the send path. Every outbound frame, text, pong, and the final close, flows through one writer in the order it pulls from the outbound channel, so the close frame is necessarily the last thing written and nothing races past it. With Arc<Mutex<sink>> shared across many tasks, the order in which writers acquire the lock is whatever the scheduler decides; a task can grab the lock and write a frame after another task has already sent close, which is a protocol violation that is hard to even observe after the fact.

Cancellation and shutdown stage more easily in the split design because there is a single place to drain. You signal shutdown (the chapter uses a watch channel), the application loop stops accepting inbound work, and the writer drains its remaining outbound queue and then sends close. With a shared sink there is no single drain point: each task may still be mid-write when you tear down, so 'finish what is in flight, then close' has no natural seam.

Slow-consumer backpressure is easier to measure in the split design because the outbound channel is the one chokepoint. A bounded outbound channel gives you a single queue depth to watch and a single place where send() blocks or fails when the client falls behind. With a shared sink, backpressure is smeared across every task that holds the lock; there is no single number that says 'this connection is behind.'

A shared sink is still acceptable when writes are rare, unordered relative to each other, and not part of a strict close sequence, for example a low-frequency metrics or keepalive emitter where no two writes have an ordering relationship and the connection never needs a clean drained close. Even then it is a deliberate exception, not the default.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One writer task owns frame ordering and the close seam; a shared sink scatters both.
criteria: Names a concrete win of split ownership: a single writer guarantees close is the last frame and ordering is deterministic.
Names a concrete cost of the shared sink: scheduler-dependent lock order can let a frame race past close, and there is no single drain seam.
Ties the comparison to ordering (close sequencing), shutdown (single drain point), and observability (one bounded queue depth), not to syntax.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement a small message loop with explicit read/write ownership
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Build the reader-app-writer pipeline the chapter's Example 1 demonstrates, but keep the focus on the ownership shape rather than on any particular WebSocket crate. Three tasks, two bounded channels, one shutdown signal.

The reader task is the only consumer of inbound frames from the transport boundary; it translates wire frames into an InboundFrame enum and pushes them onto the inbound channel. The application task is the only thing that interprets protocol, it reacts to Text, Ping, and Close distinctly, and it produces OutboundFrame values onto the outbound channel. The writer task is the only producer onto the transport; it drains the outbound channel in order. No task except the writer ever touches the send half, which is exactly the boundary that makes close ordering and backpressure tractable.

Keep the inbound and outbound enums separate. They are not the same alphabet: a Ping is inbound transport liveness and a Pong is the outbound reply; conflating them into one enum invites a task to construct a frame that only the other side should send. Two bounded channels (the chapter uses capacity 4) give you backpressure in both directions, if the application falls behind the reader, recv pressure builds on the inbound channel; if the client falls behind the writer, send pressure builds on the outbound channel.

Close is handled by signaling shutdown after the close frame is observed, not by abruptly dropping a task. When the application sees InboundFrame::Close it sends an OutboundFrame::Close so the writer can flush a clean close, then flips the watch channel to true. The writer, on seeing shutdown, drains any frames still queued and then exits. That ordering, observe close, emit close, drain, exit, is why the lifecycle is reviewable from the types alone.

On the borrowing prompt: do not move borrowed request-local data into a spawned task. Tokio's spawn requires 'static futures, so anything captured must be owned (a String, an Arc, an mpsc::Sender), not a reference into the handshake's stack frame. The connection will outlive that frame by hours, so a borrow there would be a use-after-free that the lifetime checker correctly rejects; owning the data, or sharing it behind Arc, is what makes the spawn legal and the lifecycle sound.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Reader to app to writer over two bounded channels, with a watch signal staging the close.
criteria: Read and write ownership are explicit: only the reader reads the transport and only the writer touches the send half.
Application logic sits between IO; it owns all protocol reactions and never writes to the transport directly.
Ping and Close are matched as distinct arms: Ping produces a Pong, Close emits Close and signals shutdown.
Lifecycle is reviewable from types and channels alone: two bounded enums, two channels, one watch signal; spawned tasks capture owned data, not request-local borrows.

exerciseSolutions.title: Replace unbounded broadcast with a bounded slow-consumer policy
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is named directly in the chapter: an unbounded per-client queue is not the absence of a slow-consumer policy, it is the policy 'grow memory until the process dies.' The room broadcaster pushes every event onto an unbounded VecDeque per client and only notices when RSS climbs, which means the failure is invisible until it is catastrophic and unattributable to a specific client.

The fix has two parts: a boundedness rule and a slow-consumer policy. For the boundedness rule, put the first bound per connection, because a single slow tab is the most common failure and a per-connection cap is the honest minimum. A per-room cap is a useful second bound (one runaway room should not be allowed to consume all server memory across its members), so 'both' is the mature answer, but if you only get one, make it per-connection.

For the policy, I would choose by message class rather than apply one rule everywhere, because there is no neutral slow-consumer policy and each choice changes product semantics. For a live state feed where only the newest value matters (cursor position, presence, a progress percentage), coalesce to one latest snapshot, the queue holds at most one entry and a slow client gets the freshest state, not a backlog of stale ones. For an ordered event log where every event matters (chat messages, audit events), you cannot silently drop, so the policy is bound the queue and disconnect the client at the limit, then let it reconnect and resume from a durable cursor. Dropping oldest events silently is the worst option for an event log because the client never learns it missed something. The lab makes the disconnect-at-limit policy concrete: a client already at max_pending is evicted on the next push rather than allowed to grow.

Metrics and tests close the loop. The metrics that should spike first are per-connection (and per-room) pending queue depth and queue age (how long the oldest unsent event has waited), plus an eviction or drop counter labeled by reason. Active connection count alone will not move when one client falls behind; queue depth and age will. The regression test asserts the policy mechanically: construct a hub with a small bound, seed one client at the limit, broadcast, and assert that client was evicted (or its queue was coalesced) and the bound was never exceeded, exactly the shape of the lab. The trap to avoid is replacing an unbounded VecDeque with a 'large' bounded one and calling it fixed; a bound of 100000 is still effectively unbounded for the failure you are defending against. The bound must be small enough that the policy actually fires under realistic slowness.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Per-connection bound with a policy selected by message class, plus the regression test that proves it fires.
criteria: One explicit boundedness rule stated: per-connection cap as the minimum, per-room as the second bound.
One slow-consumer policy chosen and justified by product semantics: coalesce-latest for state feeds, disconnect-at-limit for ordered event logs.
At least one metric (per-connection queue depth/age, eviction counter) and one regression test (bound-is-enforced) are named.
Explicitly rejects 'just make the bound huge' as leaving the queue unbounded under another name.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a production WebSocket protocol with versioning, auth, and shutdown semantics
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Make the envelope and lifecycle explicit before mixed clients force the decision in an incident. The chapter's framing is that a WebSocket protocol drifts the same way an HTTP API or broker envelope drifts, old clients and new servers coexist for as long as a tab stays open, so the contract belongs in the envelope, not implicit in code.

Envelope: every frame is a versioned, tagged envelope. Mandatory fields are protocol version (so a new server can detect and reject or downgrade an old client deterministically), a type tag (so the enum is a tagged union and new variants are additive), and a session ID (the stable identity that survives reconnects and ties logs together). Per-stream sequence numbers are mandatory for any ordered subscription because resume depends on them. A trace ID is strongly recommended on every message for cross-system correlation. Concretely, model it as Envelope<T> { version, type, session_id, seq, trace_id, payload: T } with #[serde(tag = "type")] on the payload enum so adding a variant never breaks old clients, which is exactly the serde shape the chapter sketches.

Layer separation: keep transport/control messages distinct from domain events. Transport-layer messages are Subscribe, Subscribed, Resume, Ack, Ping, Pong, Error, and the terminal GoingAway/Close. Domain-layer messages are the actual events the product carries (TaskProgress, Notification, and so on) wrapped in the same envelope. This separation lets the connection machinery handle liveness, resume, and shutdown without parsing domain payloads, and lets domain handlers ignore transport bookkeeping.

Reconnect and resume: the client persists the last applied (stream, seq). On reconnect it sends Resume { session_id, last_seq } per stream. If the server can still serve from that cursor (events retained in a bounded ring or a backing log), it replays from last_seq + 1; if the cursor is too old to honor, it responds with a Snapshot of current state plus a new baseline seq, and the client discards its stale assumptions. The rule the chapter insists on: this resume cursor is product liveness and is separate from ping/pong transport liveness, do not let one stand in for the other.

Shutdown: during a deploy drain the server first stops admitting new subscriptions, then sends an explicit terminal control frame, GoingAway { reason: "deploy", reconnect_after_ms, resume_supported: true }, before it closes the socket, so clients reconnect with jittered backoff and resume rather than hammering instantly. The terminal event is in the protocol from day one precisely because the server will eventually drain.

Authorization and origin: authenticate at the handshake where ordinary HTTP cookies and headers exist, validate the Origin header against an allowlist to refuse cross-site upgrades, and re-check authorization at subscribe time per tenant rather than trusting the handshake to settle authority for the connection's whole multi-hour life. Carry the tenant in the session and verify each Subscribe against it, because proving identity once does not prove continued authority to a given tenant's stream.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A versioned Envelope<T> with serde-tagged control and domain enums; control carries resume and the terminal GoingAway drain frame.
criteria: Defines one versioned envelope contract: Envelope<T> with mandatory version, session_id, seq, plus trace_id, and serde(tag) for additive evolution.
Transport/control messages (Subscribe, Resume, Ping/Pong, GoingAway) are separated from domain events (TaskProgress, Notification) explicitly.
States one resume rule (replay from last_seq, else Snapshot baseline) and one shutdown rule (stop admission, send GoingAway, then close).
Includes authorization/origin decisions: Origin allowlist at handshake plus per-tenant re-check at Subscribe time.

exerciseSolutions.title: Test disconnect storms, reconnects, and long-lived shutdown behavior
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Split the matrix into deterministic logic tests and metric-driven storm diagnosis, because storm handling is partly a test problem and partly an observability problem, and confirm both rather than relying on 'it reconnected once on my laptop.'

Deterministic tests cover the pure protocol logic where there is no excuse for flakiness: the protocol state machine (legal and illegal transitions), the resume rule (resume from a known cursor replays exactly the missing events; a too-old cursor yields a snapshot baseline), bounded queue enforcement (the lab's shape, a client at the limit is evicted and the bound is never exceeded), and graceful close ordering (admission stops, the terminal frame is emitted, then the socket closes). All of these are synchronous or controllable and should be plain unit and integration tests with asserted outcomes.

To simulate slow consumers and a drained shutdown in CI without wall-clock sleeps, drive time and IO explicitly. Model the slow consumer as a client whose receiver simply does not drain, then call broadcast and assert the queue hit the bound and the eviction fired, no sleeping, just a queue you control. For timing-dependent paths use a virtual clock (tokio's start_paused / advance, or an injected Clock trait) so a 30-second heartbeat timeout or a reconnect backoff is tested by advancing time programmatically, which is deterministic and instant. For the drain, trigger the shutdown signal directly and assert the sequence of emitted frames (admission rejected, GoingAway sent, close sent) rather than racing a real timer. This is how the plan avoids the timing lottery: time is an input, not a real-world wait.

The metrics that prove a disconnect storm is under control are reconnect rate (sustained spike means a flapping load balancer or a thundering reconnect), handshake error rate (auth or origin failures climbing during the storm), queue age and pending depth per connection and per tenant (the early warning that a consumer is behind), and per-tenant active connection count (so one tenant's storm is distinguishable from a global one). Together these are well over the three-hook minimum and they let you attribute a storm to a tenant or a path rather than just observing aggregate pain.

For attribution after the fact, every connection log and trace must carry stable IDs: session_id (survives reconnects so one client's whole reconnect history is one thread), tenant_id, and a trace_id per request/frame, plus the close reason on every disconnect. A single failed reconnect path is only debuggable later if those IDs were emitted at the time; without session_id you cannot even tell that ten log lines belong to one flapping client.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Deterministic queue-bound and shutdown-ordering tests; timeouts use a paused virtual clock, never real sleeps.
criteria: Includes deterministic tests for both the bounded queue (eviction at limit) and shutdown ordering (admission halts before close).
Names well over three observability hooks: reconnect rate, handshake error rate, per-connection/per-tenant queue age and depth, per-tenant active connections.
Includes stable ID fields for logs/traces: session_id, tenant_id, trace_id, plus the close reason.
Explains avoiding timing-lottery sleeps via an undrained queue for slow consumers and a paused virtual clock for timeouts and backoff.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab converts the unbounded fan-out from the starter code into a bounded, slow-consumer-aware hub. The one change that matters is the capacity check inside broadcast: before pushing a payload onto a client's pending queue, it reads that queue's length and compares it against max_pending. A client already at the bound is treated as too slow for the current policy and evicted (removed from the map and recorded in evicted), rather than being allowed to grow its queue without limit. That is the chapter's point made mechanical: an unbounded queue is a policy that says 'grow memory until the process dies,' and replacing it with disconnect-at-limit makes the slow consumer visible the moment it falls behind.

Ids are collected into a sorted snapshot before iterating so that eviction order is deterministic; HashMap iteration order is unspecified, and the expected output names evicted clients in a fixed order (beta,gamma), so sorting is what makes the test reproducible. Trace the two broadcasts with max_pending = 2 and initial queue depths alpha=0, beta=2, gamma=1. On broadcast("first"), sorted order is alpha, beta, gamma: alpha (len 0) accepts and delivered becomes 1; beta (len 2) is at the limit and is evicted; gamma (len 1) accepts and delivered becomes 2, growing to len 2. On broadcast("second"), the surviving clients are alpha and gamma: alpha (len 1) accepts and delivered becomes 3; gamma (now len 2) is at the limit and is evicted.

After both broadcasts, only alpha remains, so active = 1; the eviction log is beta then gamma, so evicted = beta,gamma; and exactly three pushes succeeded, so delivered = 3. The program uses only std (HashMap, VecDeque, Vec, String) and prints precisely the expected three lines.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is one writer task usually calmer than many tasks sharing the write half directly?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because a single writer is the only thing that touches the send path, it imposes one deterministic order on outbound frames: text, pongs, and the final close all flow through it in the order pulled from the outbound channel, so close is necessarily last and nothing races past it. With many tasks sharing an Arc<Mutex<sink>>, the order in which they acquire the lock is the scheduler's choice, so a stray frame can be written after close, and there is no single seam at which to drain on shutdown. It also gives you one chokepoint, the bounded outbound channel, where backpressure and queue depth are measurable, instead of pressure smeared across every lock holder.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes queue age or pending depth more actionable than active connection count alone?
reviewAnswers.answer: Active connection count does not move when a client falls behind, a slow consumer is still connected, so the number that should warn you stays flat while memory climbs. Queue age (how long the oldest unsent event has waited) and pending depth (how many events are backed up) rise immediately and point at the specific connection or tenant that is too slow for the current policy. They are leading indicators tied to the actual failure, whereas connection count is a lagging aggregate that only changes after you have already started disconnecting clients.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are reconnect and resume protocol decisions separate from ping or pong liveness?
reviewAnswers.answer: Ping and pong are transport liveness, they only tell you the socket is still open and the peer is responsive at the TCP/WebSocket layer. Reconnect and resume are product liveness, they answer which application events a client has actually applied and which it still needs after a gap, using a durable sequence cursor or last-seen sequence number. A connection can be perfectly alive by ping/pong while the client is hours behind on events, and a client can be fully caught up by cursor while a single missed pong tears the socket down, so conflating the two lets one silently stand in for the other and hides real data loss behind a healthy heartbeat.

reviewAnswers.question: When is SSE a better answer than WebSockets even if the product still wants live updates?
reviewAnswers.answer: When the direction is one-way: the client only ever listens and never needs to push commands back over the same connection. Server-Sent Events deliver server-to-client push over plain HTTP with automatic browser reconnection and a built-in Last-Event-ID resume cursor, so you avoid the entire WebSocket upgrade, split, heartbeat, and close lifecycle and the slow-consumer machinery that comes with owning a duplex connection. The tradeoff is that SSE is one-directional and text-framed, so the moment the client must send interactive commands, a WebSocket becomes the right tool again.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should graceful shutdown for long-lived sockets stop admission before closing active connections?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because shutdown is an ordering problem, and the order is stop admitting new work, drain what is in flight, then cancel the rest with a deadline, the same sequence TCP services and brokers use. If you do not stop admission first, new connections and subscriptions keep arriving while you are trying to drain, so the in-flight set never settles and the drain never completes. And if you drop the runtime out from under active sockets instead of closing them in order, your close policy, the terminal GoingAway frame, reconnect advice, and clean close, never actually runs, so clients see abrupt resets and reconnect in a thundering herd rather than backing off with resume.
